payload.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=automated+reasoning+self+correction+false+premises+validation+failure+modes&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9780203435854-18\", \"title\": [\"Conditional reasoning with false premises\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203435854-18\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2002, 9, 26]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"title\": [\"Automated Oversight Diagnostic Self-Correction and Failure-Aware Reasoning for GUI Agents(ChinaMM)\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The rapid evolution of Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) has significantly advanced autonomous GUI agents. However, during the development of GUI agents for dynamic scenarios, error compounding leads to a labor-intensive and expensive bottleneck, requiring high costs for manual intervention. Meanwhile, errors are hard to be located and difficult to track failure reasoning. Consequently, it is challenging to overcome random errors simply by blindly increasing the size of the training dataset and address errors in a targeted manner. Existing research primarily attempt to improve GUI agent by optimizing the agent&apos;s internal design to avoid outcome deviation, ignoring the critical need for automated self-correction in step-level agent errors. In view of this, we propose the Automated Oversight (AO), an efficient four-stage closed-loop approach designed to emulate human-level oversight. The architecture consists of four key phases: (1) global outcome verification for final-state checking; (2) step-level visual trajectory alignment to intercept errors in real-time; (3) teacher-driven root-cause diagnosis to analyze failures; and (4) closed-loop rectification with state rollback to recover the task. Unlike traditional methods, AO focuses on failure-aware reasoning to identify the root causes of errors and execute targeted recovery. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can improve agent success rates and reduce human cognitive burden by achieving reliable autonomous interactions in dynamic systems. We will publicly release our code.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9780203435854_chapter_13\", \"title\": [\"Conditional reasoning with false premises\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203435854_chapter_13\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01526.x\", \"title\": [\"Conditional Reasoning With False Premises Facilitates the Transition Between Familiar and Abstract Reasoning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n                  <jats:p>Abstract reasoning is critical for science and mathematics, but is very difficult. In 3 studies, the hypothesis that alternatives generation required for conditional reasoning with false premises facilitates abstract reasoning is examined. Study 1 (n = 372) found that reasoning with false premises improved abstract reasoning in 12- to 15-year-olds. Study 2 (n = 366) found a positive effect of simply generating alternatives, but only in 19-year-olds. Study 3 (n = 92) found that 9- to 11-year-olds were able to respond logically with false premises, whereas no such ability was observed in 6- to 7-year-olds. Reasoning with false premises was found to improve reasoning with semiabstract premises in the older children. These results support the idea that alternatives generation with false premises facilitates abstract reasoning.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01526.x\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2011, 3, 1]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "fd62a28fe014e3a6e3e8482d7c3fbcbd7ba3782f1c8f45e163fae77d174abd5e", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.4324/9780203435854-18", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6991012", "doi:10.4324/9780203435854_chapter_13", "doi:10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01526.x"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203435854-18", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6991012", "https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203435854_chapter_13", "https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01526.x"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
